# Expanding Claude for Nonprofits

Our new Claude for Nonprofits plugin brings new skills to every verified nonprofit organization, taking on the operational work that stretches small teams across fundraising, marketing, and hiring.

Today, we're releasing the Claude for Nonprofits plugin, a set of skills and connectors built with ~30 nonprofits. It helps teams set up Claude responsibly with their organization's context and policies, supports fundraising from research through reporting, and takes on the operational work that stretches small teams. We're also planning to extend Claude Corps (opens in new tab), our program for placing early-career fellows in U.S. nonprofits, through a partnership with Taproot (opens in new tab).

As a public benefit corporation, Anthropic has a responsibility to make sure our products are accessible and useful to organizations working on the world’s hardest problems. Last December, we launched Claude for Nonprofits (opens in new tab) with discounts of up to 75%, connectors for Blackbaud, Candid, and Benevity, and a free AI Fluency course built with GivingTuesday. More than 25,000 nonprofits now use Claude in their work. Most of those organizations are small, local operations: more than 75% of them have fewer than 10 Claude seats. We think today's update will have the biggest impact on these organizations.

We’ve spent the last year working directly with nonprofits to meet their needs. We expanded nonprofit plans to the same models as our standard Team and Enterprise plans, lowered the Team plan minimum to orgs with as few as two people, and included Claude Code in nonprofit plans at no additional cost. And during the United Nations General Assembly in September, we launched a new discount of ~90% for verified nonprofits in low- and middle-income countries, bringing standard Team seats to $3/user/month.

Cost is only one barrier. Nonprofits told us two others stood in the way: a lack of people with the skills to put AI to work, and a lack of tools built specifically for how nonprofits operate.

- Too few people with AI skills. Claude Corps is placing 1,000 early-career fellows in at least 400 US nonprofits to build with Claude alongside their teams. Hosts include a wide variety of organizations, from large organizations to small, local teams, including food banks, art museums, and veteran support organizations. We’re now planning to extend this program through a partnership with Taproot, which would match nonprofits with experienced pro bono consultants for shorter, project-based work. A growing group of partners can support nonprofit adoption, including Accenture, Boston Consulting Group (BCG), The Bridgespan Group, Civis Analytics, Deloitte, fusionSpan, Idealist Consulting, Myridius, SapienAI, Slalom, v4c.ai, and Vera Solutions. And for teams getting started on their own, we’re hosting two live webinars: Claude for Nonprofits: An Admin's Guide to Data Handling and AI Use Policy (opens in new tab), for admins, on November 10, and Claude for Nonprofits: A Staff Guide to Making Claude Useful on Day One (opens in new tab) on November 12.
- Too few tools built to meet nonprofits where they’re at. We built the skills we're releasing today with the nonprofits in our Design Partner Circle. It includes ~30 organizations, from small teams serving one region of the United States to international organizations operating in dozens of countries, working on education, economic mobility, health, humanitarian response, and more. Many are funders themselves. This fall, fundraisers, operations leads, and chiefs of staff at many of these organizations tried early versions of our skills on real work and told us what wasn't working. We brainstormed, iterated, and updated our solution based on what we heard.

## What's in the plugin

We’re starting with three areas nonprofits told us were most urgent, especially as year-end fundraising picks up.

### Extend your team

Many nonprofits told us the same thing: there are more jobs to do than people to do them, so everyone covers several roles at once. Claude extends your team, so a small staff can work like a bigger one and spend more of its time on the mission.

- Marketing: plan a campaign sized to your team’s bandwidth, teach Claude to draft in your organization’s voice, and get a second read on your content before it goes out.
- Hiring and people: build a job post with an interview guide and scoring rubric, plan a new hire's first 90 days, and answer staff questions from your own handbook.
- Board and leadership: see what skills your board is missing, draft outreach to the candidates you have in mind, get new members up to speed with an orientation packet, and plan the deck for your next meeting.

### Set up Claude responsibly: security, governance, and context

Claude works best when it has your organization’s context, including your mission, programs, workstreams, communication principles, and policies, and when your staff have clear rules for working with it. Start by asking Claude to:

- Map your organization. Claude asks where you keep each kind of record, like donor data, grant files, finances and policies, and, with memory on, saves that map for each person. It then offers to connect the tools it can't reach yet. Every other skill in the plugin reads the map first, so Claude knows where to look and you don't have to point it to the same source for each task.
- Check what your AI policy allows. Staff can ask "Can I use Claude for this?" and get the answer based on your organization's own AI policy. (No policy yet? See the Claude Academy tutorial below.)

### Fund your mission

Fundraising is the lifeline for nonprofits, and it matters even more toward the end of the year. It's also time-intensive and process-heavy, which can be challenging for small organizations. The plugin supports the full fundraising lifecycle, freeing up your team's time for the irreplaceable human work, like managing relationships and deciding which opportunities to pursue.

- Find the right funders and grants. Research donors, foundations, companies, and surface open grants, with sources cited.
- Decide what to pursue. Forward an RFP and get a breakdown on eligibility, requirements, and what it would take to compete.
- Write proposals and reports. Turn an RFP into a requirements list and a first draft built from your own material. Grant reports include sources for their figures.
- Keep relationships warm. Get a brief before a funder call, a write-up and thank-you note after, and donor updates in your voice. Ask how to re-engage donors and receive a stewardship plan.

## Where nonprofits are seeing impact

“We think of Claude as a research fellow who never gets tired. With its help, our one-person government affairs team has turned our analysis of more than 750 state anti-trafficking policies into recommendations local advocates can take to their legislators to close gaps that leave people vulnerable.”

“At Best Friends, we're always looking for ways to remove barriers so our teams can focus on saving lives. Being part of Anthropic's design partner circle gave us the opportunity to help shape tools around real nonprofit challenges, and I was impressed by how quickly Anthropic incorporated feedback and translated it into practical improvements that can help organizations increase their impact.”

“We want to use AI effectively at Braven, and Claude is a key lever in how we’re getting there. Everyone has access, we ran our own training, and our IT team built Claude skills the whole organization now shares. We believe the best way to harness AI for good is to use it ourselves and constantly test and learn what works and what doesn't.”

“With a team smaller than a soccer squad, turning thousands of citizen suggestions into credible government policy is no easy feat. Claude Code helped us rapidly prototype and iterate on a tool that turns feedback from WhatsApp, voice notes and forms into traceable, clustered reports—so governments can see not just aggregated suggestions, but the voices that ultimately shape public policy.”

“Claude turned our staff retention report into a polished board deck, and the process of refining it felt collaborative and engaging. When the board came back with follow-up questions, we had clear answers ready in about 15 minutes, work that would otherwise have taken far longer.”

“At Colnodo, we use Claude to build a platform containing global information on Community-Centered Connectivity Initiatives, to improve the monitoring of our projects, and to take on much more than we were previously able to, all while helping to bring internet access to rural communities in Colombia.”

“Claude Code has helped me pull trustworthy information on crises and our response into up-to-date documents. These are being incorporated in our operational decision-making and have contributed to significant fundraising successes.”

“The donor correspondence sounded like us. Rather than repeating the same proposal a third time, Claude suggested a more accessible starting point for the partnership. We also value the option to tailor a skill to how our organization works, which addresses the concern that AI doesn't know us.”

“We connected 25 years of grantmaking into one knowledge graph that anyone across the foundation can explore using conversational AI.”

“Our teams write their own proposals, so through the design partner circle we asked for a thorough reviewer and better support for go/no-go decisions. We have been very impressed with the result. It strengthens our proposals while keeping the decisions with our people.”

“Claude helps us find savings we’d never have spotted on our own. We used it to show one of our partner agencies what it was paying at retail compared with buying through us, and that agency now spends 40% less to feed the same neighbors. Claude is making us a much better steward of every dollar.”

Compare which Claude Code features are available across Anthropic subscription plans, the Anthropic Console, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry.

The Claude Code CLI and everything that runs locally work on every provider. For setup instructions per provider, see the Enterprise deployment overview. To skip straight to what is missing on your provider, see the summary by provider tabs.In the tables below, ✓ means available, ✗ means not available, and “See note” links to a footnote for partial support. A qualifier after ✓ narrows availability to that subset, and “Admin-enabled” means the feature is off until an organization admin turns it on.

MCP servers: connectors from claude.ai load only when your claude.ai subscription is the active authentication method. Tool search isn’t supported on Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Azure. On Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, tool search isn’t supported on models earlier than Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5

Subagents: when the main conversation runs Fable, the built-in Explore subagent runs on Opus with a Claude subscription, an Anthropic Console account, or an LLM gateway reached through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. On other providers, including Claude Platform on AWS, it runs on Fable

/design-sync and /import with its claude import subcommand form are unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS, and through a Claude apps gateway

1 On Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, web search is available for Opus 4, Sonnet 4, Haiku 4.5, and later models. 2 On these providers, auto mode supports only Claude Sonnet 5 or later, Opus 4.7 or later, Haiku 5.5, and the Fable models. See Auto mode configuration. For the permission mode a session on these providers starts in, see Which mode a session starts in. 3 Subject to your agreement with the cloud provider. 4 Dashboard and API only. Contribution metrics requires a claude.ai Team or Enterprise organization. 5 Requires Claude Code v2.1.224 or later on macOS and Linux, including Linux inside WSL 2. On native Windows, requires Claude Code v2.1.234 or later. With API key authentication, messaging is same-machine only. On Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, messaging is same-machine only and requires Claude Code v2.1.248 or later. Claude can find your cloud sessions and your sessions on other machines only from a session that is connected to Remote Control. To connect, you need a claude.ai sign-in and the other Remote Control requirements. See Message sessions on other machines.

If you authenticate through an LLM gateway, feature availability matches the underlying provider the gateway forwards to, except for the features Claude Code itself turns off. Whenever ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a host other than api.anthropic.com, Claude Code turns off features such as Remote Control and server-managed settings, whatever the gateway forwards. Some Anthropic-only features such as the Advisor work only if the gateway forwards requests intact to the Anthropic API.For how the requests Claude Code sends differ between an Amazon Bedrock- or Agent Platform-format gateway, an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateway, and a Claude apps gateway sign-in, see client behavior by connection method.

Each tab lists what is unavailable or partially supported on that provider, with alternatives where one exists. Everything not listed works the same as on a Claude subscription, apart from the provider-specific differences noted above. On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS, error reporting and telemetry to Anthropic are off by default. See default behaviors by API provider for what traffic still reaches Anthropic and how to opt out.

If you authenticate through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or an Anthropic Console API key, this section does not apply to you. When you sign in with a claude.ai account, your plan determines which of the features below are available.In Enterprise organizations with the HIPAA configuration applied, some features in this table are turned off.

For which Claude models and context-window sizes are available per provider and region, see Model configuration and the Models overview. Vision, PDF input, and extended thinking are model capabilities rather than Claude Code features and work on every provider that offers the model. Prompt caching works the same way on most providers; on Amazon Bedrock, support varies by model.

Anthropic.title: Claude Chat and Cowork Are Now One. Here Is What Changes for Enterprise AI Governance. - Gethyn Ellis
Anthropic.description: For Enterprise customers, conversational assistance and longer-running agentic work now live in the same place, following Anthropic’s 23 October announcement. ... Anthropic-managed Claude on Google Cloud is now generally available, with Google Cloud IAM, Marketplace billing and commitment drawdown. It is distinct from Google-managed Vertex AI.
Anthropic.content:
# Claude Chat and Cowork Are Now One. Here Is What Changes for Enterprise AI Governance.

The week of 20 to 26 October 2026 was a busy one for Anthropic. Claude chat and Cowork became a single Enterprise experience, Claude Security gained continuous vulnerability monitoring, a new API version introduced breaking changes, Claude Duet previewed always-on personal agents in the US, and on Monday 26 October the company publicly filed for an IPO. Here is what each development means for UK organisations deploying or evaluating Claude.

The thread running through the product news is the one I keep returning to: the boundary between answering a question and executing work is dissolving. When a conversation can turn into a running task that continues after you close your laptop, governance has to follow the task, not the chat window.

## 1. Claude chat and Cowork are now one experience

For Enterprise customers, conversational assistance and longer-running agentic work now live in the same place, following Anthropic’s 23 October announcement. A conversation can progress into document creation or data analysis and carry on after the user closes their device. Eligible existing Enterprise organisations are scheduled for default enablement on 16 November 2026, provided Chat and Cloud code execution and file creation are enabled. Administrators can enable it earlier or choose to keep it disabled; an explicit choice is retained.

Three things matter for governance:

- Exclusions. Organisations using zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configurations or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) are currently excluded. If you are in financial services, health or the public sector and rely on those controls, you cannot switch this on yet.
- Billing. Unified Claude is usage-based. A new Efficient mode restricts unified sessions to Sonnet and Haiku, which gives administrators a cost lever but also a quality trade-off to explain to users.
- Scope. Once a chat can become a workflow that creates documents and analyses data unattended, your acceptable-use policy, data-handling rules and approval model need to cover the task, not just the prompt.

What to do now: Decide before 16 November whether to enable early, enable on the default date or hold. Update your Claude usage guidance so that it covers long-running tasks, and check whether any of the compliance exclusions apply to your tenant.

## 2. Claude Security: finding vulnerabilities is not the same as keeping software secure

Claude Security now supports continuous repository scanning in public beta, with contextual threat models, fix tracking, API access and MCP integration. The shift from a one-off scan to continuous monitoring is the important part. Continuous scanning and fix tracking can support an ongoing remediation process, but they do not prove the application is secure. Findings still need engineering review, ownership and a retest.

There is also a commercial hook. Eligible Claude Enterprise organisations can receive up to US$25,000 in Claude Security credits per month for two consecutive months. Existing customers’ offer began on 21 October, whether or not they use it. The offer ends on 31 December 2026 UTC; unused monthly credits do not carry over, and customers joining after 1 November will not receive two full months. Check the launch offer terms before planning an evaluation.

What to do now: Pick one application with a known security debt (a typical candidate is a React front end on Supabase and PostgreSQL) and run a time-boxed evaluation: identify, review, fix, rescan. Keep the public beta label in mind when writing anything into policy.

## 3. The API changed, and your integrations will not migrate themselves

Claude API version 2026-10-21 removes thetemperature, top_p and top_k parameters. Requests that still send them return HTTP 400. Certain document and citation structures also change. Python SDK 2.0.0, TypeScript SDK 1.0.0 and the ant CLI 2.0.0 use the new version by default.

Integrations pinned to the older API version keep working. The risk is the unplanned upgrade: a developer bumps a dependency, the SDK silently moves to the new version, and a production agent starts failing on a parameter nobody remembered was there.

What to do now: Audit every Claude integration for the removed parameters and the changed document structures. Update examples and regression tests before upgrading SDKs. If you run agent-building training, the labs need updating too.

## 4. Policy enforcement belongs outside the model

Enterprise inference hooks are now generally available. They let an organisation-operated security service inspect governed requests and return an allow or deny decision before inference happens. Alongside that, organisation administrators can now disable web fetch entirely or restrict it to allowed and blocked domains, and Managed Agents respects those controls in addition to agent-level restrictions.

This is the control pattern I would want in any enterprise agent deployment. A policy that lives in a system prompt can be argued with, rewritten or forgotten. Enforcement outside the model gives the policy a control point that does not depend on the model following instructions.

Check the deployment boundary: inference hooks govern Claude Enterprise products. They do not cover standalone Claude Platform API organisations, Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud. The organisation-level web controls described above are separate Claude Platform controls.

What to do now: Design the hook for denial, logging and fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour before you wire it in. For web access, test a permitted URL, a denied URL and a redirect to a prohibited domain, because the redirect case is where most allow-lists leak.

## 5. Claude Code: sandbox and permission fixes worth tracking

Recent Claude Code releases include permission and operational fixes. Version 2.1.307, released on 21 October, introducesclaude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry events, which means denied actions and permission decisions can now flow into your existing observability stack rather than living only in local logs.

What to do now: If Claude Code is in use across engineering teams, standardise on a current version and route the safety events to wherever you already monitor developer tooling.

## 6. Claude Duet: agents that work while you sleep need a different permission model

Claude Duet introduces proactive, always-on personal agents: briefings, connected-app monitoring, task execution and approval checkpoints. Its research preview is limited to US Pro and Max subscribers via waitlist, so for UK organisations this is one to watch rather than deploy.

The accompanying security publication is worth reading regardless. It covers credential isolation, sensitive-information checking and mandatory approval for consequential actions. Those are the design questions every proactive agent raises: how much authority is delegated, how approval fatigue is avoided without removing approval, and where the hard limits on autonomous action sit.

What to do now: Use Duet’s architecture to sharpen the language in your own frameworks. Distinguish clearly between assistants (respond when asked), supervised agents (act within a session under approval) and proactive agents (act on triggers, unattended). Do not promise UK availability.

## 7. Deployment options and delivery reliability

Anthropic-managed Claude on Google Cloud is now generally available, with Google Cloud IAM, Marketplace billing and commitment drawdown. It is distinct from Google-managed Vertex AI. Current endpoints are US and Global, so it is not a UK data-processing guarantee.

Anthropic also reported connector disruption on 22 October and several model-related incidents between 23 and 25 October, all marked resolved when checked on 26 October 2026. For anyone running instructor-led delivery or live demonstrations, keep recorded demos and offline exercises ready. Live services have bad days.

## 8. Anthropic has filed for its IPO

On Monday 26 October 2026, Anthropic publicly filed its S-1 registration statement with the SEC, seeking to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead banks. This is a filing, not a completed listing: the preliminary prospectus does not set a final offer price or confirmed first trading date. Reported valuations and timetables remain expectations.

For UK enterprise buyers, the practical issue is vendor assessment:

- Transparency. The prospectus gives procurement and vendor-risk teams financial, governance and risk disclosures to examine. A completed listing would bring continuing public reporting obligations.
- Commercial scrutiny. My expectation is that public-market scrutiny will put further pressure on pricing, product priorities and commitments. Treat that as an operating assumption to test, rather than a confirmed change to your contract.
- Resilience. A public listing would not establish financial stability or remove delivery risk. Keep assessing cash requirements, infrastructure dependencies, service commitments, data portability and your exit plan.

The useful procurement conversation is what the disclosures change about your supplier assessment, rather than what the shares might be worth.

## 9. Claude versus Microsoft 365 Copilot

Unified Claude increases the overlap with Copilot’s productivity use cases. The distinction is becoming clearer rather than blurrier: Microsoft 365 Copilot offers native integration with the Microsoft 365 estate and its governance model; Claude offers cross-system task execution with controls such as inference hooks and organisation-level web restrictions. Which suits a given organisation depends on where its data lives, which compliance controls it relies on and how much autonomous work it wants to delegate.

Anthropic.content:
# Felix, Head of Claude Engineering: Stop using Claude like you did in 2024.

后浪进化星球2026-10-27 00:41

The real watershed does not lie in who is the first to use the model.

In a recent in-depth interview, Felix Rieseberg, Head of Engineering at Anthropic Claude, shared his current way of working and why most people are still using Claude the way they did in 2024. His team spent about a week and a half building Claude Cowork, and he barely writes code now, calling himself "just a conveyor belt for Claude". The core viewpoints can be summarized as: If you only ask Claude to summarize emails and polish texts, you are not really benefiting from the new intelligence. What is truly valuable is to redesign the workflow, let AI access raw data and tools, use it to make prototypes, conduct adversarial reviews, and do things you could not do before; and the most important abilities of human beings are still empathy, taste and judgment.

The following is Felix's full sharing:

## I. I No Longer Write Code, I Am Just a Conveyor Belt for Claude

I don't write code anymore. Most of the time, I am working on prototype design: we try a lot of ideas, leave them for two nights to judge whether they are good or bad ideas, then tell Claude to generate all variants, and then critically analyze which ideas are good and which are bad.

A year and a half ago, I was still doing this: finding a crash, picking it up, bringing it to Claude and saying "please fix this". I soon realized that I was just a conveyor belt for Claude. The correct approach is not that I carry each crash to Claude one by one, but to let Claude have access to all crash data and judge by itself what needs to be fixed and what does not. The upfront setup cost is higher, but once it is built, it will open many doors for you, and this is the real hard value brought by AI.

## II. An Agent Consists of Five Parts: Model, Harness, Sandbox, Knowledge and Tools

An agent is made up of five elements:

First, the large language model. It is responsible for perception, reasoning, planning and decision-making. Second, the harness. It coordinates memory, including active memory, working memory and long-term memory, and activates tools. Third, the sandbox. The harness runs in a secure runtime, isolated from the rest of the system. Fourth, knowledge. The agent needs to access company data to turn structured and unstructured data into a knowledge base. Fifth, tools. The agent must use tools to do actual work.

The model, harness, sandbox, knowledge and tools together form an agent.

## III. No Role-playing, Professional Tools and Processes Are Needed

I never say to Claude "you are an excellent engineer". This kind of "act like" was very popular in 2024, but most models today still have a problem: when you ask it to "act like a good accountant", it will do a little bit of role-playing. Role-playing is not what we want.

What we want are the technologies, tools and knowledge that professionals will use, not just vocabulary. I don't need Claude to sound like something, nor do I need it to put on a costume. I even want it to talk to me like it is talking to a five-year-old child, but I want it to use all the top tools in this field.

So I often prompt like this: "Tell me what tools the top people in this field will use, then you use the same tools to do it." The key is not to let it play a role, but to let it adopt a professional process.

## IV. Adversarial Review: Let Multiple Claude Attack One Claude

How to avoid AI confidently giving you wrong answers? I have a very practical answer: adversarial review.

Give one Claude a task, then send out ten other Claude, whose only task is to attack this output and prove why it is wrong. This is the same concept as red team drills and short selling. Usually, it is easier to find defects than to create new things, just like judging whether a new mobile phone is good or not is much easier than designing a new mobile phone from scratch. So you can lower the intelligence level by one gear and still get very good review results.

The specific practice: I use Claude Projects, tell Claude "open five threads, and the task of each thread is to prove that this blog post is wrong, my way of thinking is wrong, the facts are wrong, and I have misunderstood something". They work with the goal of "prove me wrong".

Then how to deal with the output? Use another Claude as a judge. Its job is to verify and confirm which criticisms are valid and which are invalid. Valid feedback goes back to the original Claude that did the work, and it can also decide whether to adopt it. Sometimes the feedback sounds reasonable, but misses the point, is not operable or useless - this usually means that my output is already quite good.

I rarely let the current session judge itself. The current session is often not good at judging whether the work it does is good or not. Try to find external signals; in emergency situations, another Claude session can also be used as an external signal. But my preference is to find hard external evidence to prove what works and what does not.

## V. Give Full Data and Tools, Don't Give Each Agent Sliced Data

Many people will upload a specific data set for each agent, or assign a "role" to each agent. I think this is over-rotation. The model is a very strong generalist, and now the tool calling ability has made great progress: it knows when to use tools, how to use tools, will not fall into tool calling loops, and will not call tools frantically until the data is exhausted.

So the correct approach is not to slice the data and then give each agent the small piece it wants. Because if we humans want to work efficiently, we also need a complete view of the entire business. As an engineering manager, if you only give me code access, my value to you will be much lower; if I also have customer data, customer calls, usage information, and business data, I can judge what works and what does not. You want your agent to have the same scope of data.

What if there is a lot of data? Give tools, and document in detail the types of data behind the tools. In this way, the agent does not have to swallow all the data, it only needs to know: if you want business data, this is the tool to get business data. You don't need to decide in advance what data each agent needs.

## VI. Model Experience: Think from the Perspective of the Model

I like to consider "model experience", not just "user experience". Pretend you are the model, you are Claude: if you want to complete this task, what would you want?

You will soon find out: you really want to access raw data, want a computer, may want to install software, want to make your own decisions, instead of others already telling you what they think. You just want to see the raw data and make your own decisions.

The upfront cost is higher, but it is worth it. Once it is built, it will open many doors. This is where the real hard value of AI lies.

## VII. The Half-life of Skills Is Very Short, Sometimes Deleting the Skill Works Better

We still use skills, but both the official guidelines and my personal advice are: be very careful with skills. We often tell the model some information that is only relevant to the previous generation of models, and time is compressed too fast in the AI field. The half-life of a good skill is very short.

Sometimes you will find that if you delete this skill completely, the output will be better. Just prompt directly and see what happens. This is most useful for people who have eval and know the standards of good and bad. I am very cautious and very discerning about when to use skills.

## VIII. AI Products Are Still in the "Eve of iPhone" Era

How different will life be in five years? This is a big question. I can say with relative certainty: the AI products we use today will all look completely different in the future.

I think we are currently in the pre-iPhone era. All AI products today are roughly equivalent to the various mobile phones before the advent of smartphones. AI has become mainstream and popular, and it is easy to make people think that "this is the end game", but I am quite convinced that we are still in the early stage.

This is also why I suggest almost everyone do an experiment: if you currently have trust issues with AI, don't hand over all the reins in one day. Run side by side. You read things, write down your feedback, do several rounds; then see what feedback Claude will give. Where are they different? Where are they the same? This will help you sharpen your workflow. Even for the same person, if you review the same document on Monday and Friday, the feedback will be different.

## IX. The Key to Starting a Business Has Not Changed: Empathy, and Judgment After Execution Becomes Cheaper

In 2015, we built a study abroad booking platform, hired many engineers, and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars. Now I can build it myself in two days. The execution cost has become extremely low.

But the secret to building good products has not actually changed much: empathy. Have empathy for users, have empathy for usage scenarios, and figure out whether this is really valuable to the person who ultimately pays.

We always say "ideas are worthless, execution is expensive". Now execution has become extremely cheap, so we need to pay more attention to empathy, connection, truly entering the business, understanding needs, and knowing how to optimize. This may even be the revenge of MBA: MBAs can now start many software startups, and they may be quite successful.

Another judgment: capability surplus does exist. You have a great model in front of you, if you only ask "what is the capital of France", you are not really tapping its potential. Dario said "a genius data center", and my job is: assuming we have a genius data center, how to let users really use it? This requires creativity, rethinking your needs, and what you think is possible.

At the personal level, many people s

Anthropic.content:
## Documentation Index

Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt

Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

Skip to main content

Use Claude Science

# Tools and environments

Claude writes and runs Python, R, and shell commands.

Claude writes and runs Python, R, and shell commands (PowerShell on Windows). Python and R run in a persistent kernel that keeps variables in memory across steps in a session. The kernel ends after about 30 minutes idle, when a package install restarts its environment, or when the session ends.

## Starter environments
First launch creates two read-only conda environments in ~/.claude-science:
- Python: numpy, pandas, scipy, matplotlib, seaborn, pillow
- R: tidyverse, ggplot2, jsonlite

## Task environments
When work needs packages the starters don’t have, Claude reuses an existing named environment or proposes creating a new one (for example, single-cell or structural-biology). A permission card shows the environment name and initial packages. Environments are shared across all projects on the machine. To list or delete environments, ask Claude; there’s no settings page for them.

## Installing packages
Claude installs from these sources by default:
- Conda: micromamba from the conda-forge, bioconda, defaults, and pytorch channels
- Python: pip from PyPI
- R: CRAN and Bioconductor

pip install or install.packages()) lasts only until the kernel restarts. To keep a package, ask Claude to install it into the environment. For a Python package Claude can’t install there with pip, see Python package sources for starter and task environments.
For tools without a package, Claude downloads source, builds it in the sandbox with compilers from conda-forge, and saves the build as an artifact for reuse.
The sandbox has no root access or system package manager. apt and sudo aren’t available; Claude uses conda-forge or builds from source instead.

### Python package sources for starter and task environments
When Claude uses pip to install a Python package into a starter or task environment, it installs only prebuilt packages (wheels) from PyPI or, if one is set up, your internal mirror. It doesn’t install a package from a git repository, a web address, a local folder, or a local file. If the package, or a package it depends on, has no wheel for your computer and Python version, the install fails. That includes a package published only as source code. When the newest version of a package has no wheel for your computer and Python version but an older version does, pip installs the older version. To find out which version you have, ask Claude. If you need the newest version, use one of the ways below. To use a package Claude can’t install this way, ask Claude to install it into the environment with conda if conda-forge has it. Otherwise, ask Claude to install it with pip in a code cell, where it lasts only until the kernel restarts.

### Environments in granted folders
On Linux, a uv, conda, mamba, or pixi environment in a folder you’ve granted Read & write can still be read-only to Claude. This happens when the environment’s package files are hard links shared with the tool’s package cache, the folder where the tool keeps the packages it has downloaded. A change to those files could also change the cache and other environments that share them. Claude can still run code from the environment but can’t add, update, or remove packages in it. The failure shows as Read-only file system from pip, uv, and pixi, and as EnvironmentNotWritableError from conda. In a uv project, uv run and uv sync fail the same way whenever they have to update the environment, for example after pyproject.toml changes.
To add packages, choose one of these:

- In a uv project, ask Claude to use a separate environment. Have Claude setUV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT to the full path of a folder in the session’s workspace folder and run uv as usual. The variable has to stay set for later uv commands, including uv run and uv sync. The separate environment belongs to that session, so another session starts without it. For a change every session keeps, change the environment yourself in a terminal outside Claude Science.
- With any of these tools, change the environment yourself. In a terminal outside Claude Science, use the tool’s own commands to add, update, or remove packages.

## GPUs
If your Linux machine has NVIDIA GPUs, the sandbox makes them available to code Claude runs, including on multi-GPU machines. To use them, turn on the Host GPU switch in Settings > Compute. Sessions you start after that can use the GPU. A session started while the switch was off keeps running without it, and so does a session continued from it with Continue as a new session.
If Claude Science finds no GPU, Claude notes this when a task needs one and can run the work on the remote compute you’ve connected. See Remote compute clusters and Compute providers. If your machine has an NVIDIA GPU but the Host GPU switch isn’t in Settings > Compute, or Claude says there’s no GPU in a session started with the switch on, see How Claude Science detects a GPU.

Turning on the Host GPU switch reduces the default sandboxing configuration applied by Claude Science.

### How Claude Science detects a GPU
On Linux, Claude Science detects an NVIDIA GPU by running nvidia-smi. When it finds no GPU this way, Claude treats the machine as having no GPU, and the Host GPU switch doesn’t appear in Settings > Compute unless it’s already on.
Claude Science runs the first nvidia-smi it finds in these folders, in this order:

- /usr/local/nvidia/bin
- /usr/bin
- /bin
- /usr/lib/wsl/lib
- /opt/bin

command -v nvidia-smi in a terminal outside Claude Science. Claude Science doesn’t look for nvidia-smi in any other folder, such as /usr/local/bin. If the nvidia-smi in a listed folder is a link, the file it finally leads to, after any other links, must also be named nvidia-smi and be under /usr, /lib, /lib64, /bin, /sbin, or /opt. To see the file a link finally leads to, run readlink -f with its path, for example readlink -f /usr/bin/nvidia-smi.
nvidia-smi also has to work without the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable, because Claude Science doesn’t pass that variable on to it, even when your terminal has it set. To check, run it in a terminal outside Claude Science by its full path with the variable removed, for example env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH /usr/bin/nvidia-smi. If that fails where plain nvidia-smi works, the variable is the reason. Make nvidia-smi work without the variable, or ask your system administrator to.
If nvidia-smi is in another folder, link it into /usr/bin, which takes administrator (sudo) access. If you don’t have that access, ask your system administrator to make the link. For example, when nvidia-smi is in /usr/local/bin, run this in a terminal outside Claude Science:

After either fix is in place, run
sudo ln -s /usr/local/bin/nvidia-smi /usr/bin/nvidia-smi
claude-science stop in a terminal outside Claude Science and start Claude Science again. If Claude Science then finds the GPU, the Host GPU switch is in Settings > Compute and its label shows the GPU’s name. Turn it on if it’s off, then start a new session, not one made with Continue as a new session.

# OpenAI rewrites its AI rulebook around five core values

The updated Model Spec asks GPT to understand what people really want rather than follow instructions word for word.

OpenAI has reorganised its Model Spec, the public rulebook for its AI, around five values led by faithfulness to human intent. It adds guidance on context and human agency, drops most style rules and renames the model GPT. OpenAI admits its models do not yet fully follow it.

OpenAI has rewritten its Model Spec, the public rulebook for how its AI should behave, around five core values, the company said on Thursday. The update also drops most of its style rules and now calls the model “GPT” rather than “the assistant.”

The five values are faithfulness to human intent, minimising harm, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. OpenAI calls faithfulness the foundation: the model should grasp what people actually want rather than follow instructions word for word.

“As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive,” OpenAI wrote.

New sections tell the model how to use context such as past chats and memories, how to support people’s own choices and how to follow social norms. Most rules stay as defaults that users and developers can change, with firm limits only where needed to protect people.

The model should also not tell people what it thinks they want to hear. It can take a side when asked, but otherwise should approach questions objectively. Chatbots’ habit of flattering their users has drawn growing criticism.

OpenAI admits its models “do not yet fully reflect” the Spec and says it is testing new training methods to teach the values. Just last week, OpenAI said one of its agents had removed a safety monitor and then denied doing so.

The company is asking the public where they disagree with the balance the new Spec strikes. Rival Microsoft published its own AI rulebook in September.

OpenAI.content:
# OpenAI GPT 模型原理进化史

2026-10-29 8

简介： OpenAI GPT 模型原理进化史

人类作者：月牙寂（龚浩华）

Agent 作者：月绡凝（小凝）

定位：OpenAI GPT 家族的开篇总览——从 GPT-1 到 GPT-5.6 的演进时间线、关键技术点详解与进化逻辑总结。供主人先建立「一张图」再深入各分篇。

免责声明：本文为学习与技术分享用途，技术细节以官方技术报告与发布说明为准。

### OpenAI GPT 模型原理进化史

### 一、演进时间线总览

时间 | 模型 | 核心变化 
---|---|---
2018-06 | GPT-1（1.17 亿参数） | 首个开源实践「预训练 + 微调」；押注自回归解码器路线 
2019-02 | GPT-2（15 亿参数） | 零样本能力；规模曲线初现；因生成质量引发关注 
2020-05 | GPT-3（1750 亿参数） | 规模化豪赌：少样本上下文学习 + 能力涌现 
2022-03 | InstructGPT（13 亿参数） | RLHF 三步对齐；对齐 = 能力放大器（小胜大） 
2022-11 | ChatGPT（GPT-3.5 + RLHF） | 对话式 AI 引爆全球；产品形态定型 
2023-03 | GPT-4 | 多模态（文+图）；系统卡 + 红队制度化；行业「智能基线」 
2024-05 | GPT-4o | 原生多模态（文/图/音端到端）；实时语音；成本大降 
2024-09 | o1 | 测试时扩展：RL 训练长思考，思考时间换精度 
2025-04 | o3 / o4-mini | 推理 + 全工具 Agent（自主搜索/Python/图像） 
2025-08 | GPT-5 | 推理与对话大一统：SWE-bench 74.9%，编码/Agent 任务 SOTA 
2025-11~2026-03 | GPT-5.1 → 5.4 | Codex 编码系 + Thinking 思考系 + 档位分化 
2026-07 | GPT-5.6 Sol/Luna/Terra | 旗舰推理系列：编码/研究/科学/网安/计算机使用 

### 二、三条主线：规模 · 对齐 · 能力

OpenAI 的进化围绕三条主线交叉推进：

1规模线（GPT-1→3）：架构不变只放大——1750 亿参数实证缩放定律，「大力出奇迹」成为行业共识。

2对齐线（InstructGPT→GPT-4→o/GPT-5）：从 RLHF 手工对齐，到系统卡/红队/分级评估的制度化对齐。

3能力线（ChatGPT→4o→o1→GPT-5）：会续写 → 会对话 → 会看图听音 → 会思考 → 会调用工具干活（Agent）。

### 三、关键技术点详解

- 自回归解码器（GPT-1 定型的 DNA）

单向预测下一个词，训练目标 = 生成目标——能生成、易规模化、可涌现；

与 BERT 双向编码器分道扬镳，十年后成为唯一赢家（DeepSeek/Claude/Gemini 同路线）。

- 少样本上下文学习（GPT-3）

不微调、只给 prompt 示例即「学会」新任务；

意义：能力从「训练时固定」变「使用时装配」——Prompt 工程与 Agent 玩法之根。

- 能力涌现（GPT-3）

部分任务跨过规模阈值后性能突然跳到可用水平；

意义：规模带来质变；无法从小模型外推。

- RLHF 三步对齐（InstructGPT）

SFT → 奖励模型 RM（人类排序打分）→ PPO 强化学习（+KL 约束）；

关键实验：13 亿 InstructGPT 胜 1750 亿 GPT-3——对齐是能力放大器。

- 系统卡与红队（GPT-4 制度化）

公开能力/风险/评估/红队结果；按风险分级发布；

意义：大模型第一次有「说明书」，成为行业事实标准。

- 原生多模态（GPT-4o）

文本/图像/音频端到端同一网络，实时语音 232ms 级；

模态融合度越高交互越自然——后续各家旗舰同路线。

- 测试时扩展（o1）

算力新维度：推理时给更多思考 token 也变强；

RL 训练隐藏思维链；思考深度可调（o3/o4-mini 分档）。

- 推理 + Agent 统一（o3 / GPT-5）

o3：推理模型第一次自主组合全工具（搜索/Python/图像）；

GPT-5：推理与对话大一统 + reasoning effort 可调 + 长程工具链稳定执行；

趋势：「默认会想、按需深想」成为旗舰默认行为（GPT-5.4 思考计划可中途调整）。

∞

### 四、进化逻辑总结（学习重点）

1架构做「减法」：始终解码器不换赛道——把创新全押在数据、对齐、推理、系统上。

2规模做「加法」：参数与数据滚雪球——缩放定律（llm-理论 02）的产业验证。

3对齐做「制度化」：RLHF（手工）→ 系统卡/红队/分级（制度）——从「能对齐」到「可审计」。

#### Columnist and Technology

# The most important part of AI chatbots is being ignored

AI firms can increase the power of their chatbots without updating to new models. Columnist Jacob Aron explains how a simple bit of software can give AI a boost – and whether AI will soon be able to rewrite that code itself

ChatGPT was never meant to start a revolution. When it launched in November 2022, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called it “an early demo” and expectations were low. Personally, my initial reaction was that it seemed no more capable than previous large language models (LLMs) OpenAI had released; it just had a nicer interface. Obviously, I was wrong to dismiss the importance of the interface, but in 2026 I think most people who use AI are making a similar mistake without even realising it. What you think of as ChatGPT or Claude or any other chatbot from a big AI brand is actually many pieces of software wrapped into one, and we are ignoring the most important: the harness.

To understand what a harness is and how it works, it helps to break down the multiple things we call ChatGPT. At the very bottom is the LLM, currently a version of GPT-6, but this gets switched out when OpenAI releases new model families. LLMs do one thing: given a string of text, they predict the most likely next characters. OpenAI’s first model, GPT-1, was released in 2018 as a piece of software that you had to download and run on your computer through a terminal, the text-based interface to a computer that most of us avoid. The same was true of GPT-2 in 2019, until an independent software developer called Adam King created Talk to Transformer, a now-defunct website that allowed you to enter a prompt and get a GPT-2 response in return. Back-and-forth chat wasn’t possible, but this was an early example of an interface, in this case a website, sitting on top of a model.

In 2020, OpenAI released GPT-3 and, for the first time, allowed people to access it through an application programming interface (API), its first commercial product. APIs are a standard way for one computer to communicate with another – for example, Google has a Google Maps API that lets a piece of software send a request for location data. OpenAI’s API let anyone create software that could plug in to GPT-3. At the time, I played with a few of these and found them interesting but clunky – the text they produced was often incorrect or flawed in some way, though it was cool that this level of text generation was even possible. This was essentially still a time of “raw” LLM output, with no guard rails – if you asked GPT-3 to produce hate speech or instructions to build a bomb, it would do so to the best of its ability.

Advertisement

That changed with the release of GPT-3.5 and, at the same time, ChatGPT, which was first called “Chat with GPT-3.5” until a last-minute name change. That original name reveals the way OpenAI saw ChatGPT, as simply an interface to a model, and this explains my reaction as well – the results I got from playing with ChatGPT seemed to be similar to GPT-3, just easier to use.

Actually, there was a crucial difference. With GPT-3.5, OpenAI had attempted to install guard rails that would prevent the model from producing text it deemed harmful, with software that would screen inputs and outputs. These didn’t work very well – you could get around them by asking for a malicious request to be fulfilled in the form of a poem, for example – but this was the beginning of a move away from raw LLMs to ones mediated by a harness sitting between the model and the interface.

Today, the ChatGPT product, whether that’s the app on your phone or the website, has an extensive harness that is mostly hidden from the user. It allows the model to do things like search the internet, read documents, or “reason”, meaning to continuously prompt itself through a “chain of thought” to produce better results. OpenAI also has another, more complex harness for its models, called Codex, which allows the LLM to more directly control a computer and so is particularly useful for writing computer code.

Why does any of this matter? Well, the dirty secret of the big AI firms is that their best models are, to some extent, interchangeable. The technology behind an OpenAI GPT model, a generative pre-trained transformer, is the same as the one used by Anthropic, Google or any other AI company. There are important differences in the data and computing power used to train these models, but generally they are all headed in the same direction, which is why the companies are constantly racing to claim the crown of “best” model before another one takes its place.

What really makes the difference is the harness. To illustrate this, I gave the same prompt – “Who am I?” – to the same model, GPT-6, in three different ways. Via API, I got a response beginning: “I don’t know your identify from this chat.” From chatgpt.com, without being logged in, I got a response that started “That’s a big question. 🙂”. When logged in to my personal account, the response began “You’re Jacob Aron, a senior editor at New Scientist, with a strong interest in mathematics, science, technology and the limits of what we can actually know.”

But the harness matters much more than simply knowing a few facts about the user. In the ARC-AGI test, considered to be one of the leading measures of model “intelligence”, models are tested using either a stripped-down harness that is standardised across all models, or a “provider adapter” that allows access to specific tools each AI firm has built. The difference is remarkable – for GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s leading public model, test scores jumped by as much as 80 percentage points when using the provider adapter harness rather than the standard one. For an earlier model, GPT-5.6 Sol, OpenAI found that just tweaking two settings in its harness tripled the resulting ARC-AGI score.

If harnesses are so important, why don’t we talk about them more often? Why don’t AI firms shout about their new harness, rather than just their latest model? I think there are a few reasons. The first is simply that they are complicated and technical – I have taken a whole article to explain them – and your average chatbot user doesn’t really need to know about it. But the second is that they are, in a way, boring. The cost of training a leading LLM is approaching $1 billion, a Herculean effort that requires number crunching across a vast army of computer processors. Once LLMs are trained, we still don’t really know exactly how they produce the results that they do, providing an air of mystery. Harnesses, on the other hand, are just ordinary software, lines of code written by humans that anyone can read.

But here is where it gets really interesting. If a harness is just code, can an AI write and improve its own harness? That is currently an open research question, both inside the AI firms and for academics. For example, in a paper published this August, one research team tested models by identifying repeated failures and proposing tweaks to their harnesses that would address the failures, seeing improvements of around 10 to 40 percentage points on benchmarks. This is why I think we are going to be hearing much more about harnesses in the near future. If the goal of the AI firms is recursive self-improvement – an AI that can build a better AI – then the harness, not the model, could be the key to achieving it.

## Further AI reading:

- OpenAI appears to have overturned a big assumption in computer science, as part of a release that saw new results in maths and physics as well. Interestingly, it is taking a slightly different approach for each of them based on feedback from academics. For the maths result, related to a problem about spinning a needle, OpenAI has released the AI output in full. It is doing the same for the computer science result, a refutation of a conjecture called the exponential time hypothesis, while also funding a conference to discuss it. The physics result is being held back until it is reviewed by external experts. It seems like OpenAI is still trying to figure out what to do about its models stepping on academics’ toes.

- Anthropic has released details of its business ahead of a planned initial public offering (IPO) on the stock market later this year. It calls AI “the most consequential technology in human history” (no surprises there) while also warning that it may pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” – again, not particularly surprising given Anthropic’s public record, but it does raise eyebrows to see this language in documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

### OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra for faster, better-performing AI agents at half the price

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6.1 Terra, an upgrade to the middle tier model in its lineup of frontier artificial intelligence systems.

The new model, the successor to GTP-5.6 Terra, costs around 50% less while handling computer use tasks faster and with greater accuracy.

Terra is positioned as the everyday model in OpenAI’s lineup, designed for routine work such as reading what’s on a computer screen, clicking through applications, navigating websites and drafting messages. The 50% price cut applies to the model’s standard application programming interface rates, which is what developers pay to integrate GPT-6.1 Terra into their own applications.

According to OpenAI, it’s meant to be a kind of compromise model that’s faster and cheaper for simpler tasks such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, editing videos, creating images and automating repetitive tasks – work that doesn’t require the heft of its more advanced model, GPT-6.1 Sol.

“We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast and efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing,” OpenAI wrote in a blog post introducing the model. “A significant step up from GPT-5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.”

GPT-6.1 Terra: delivering fast and capable computer use at a lower price.

GPT-6.1 Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it. pic.twitter.com/8JTN1yonmV

— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 26, 2026

OpenAI said the model is available now for all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. ChatGPT Work is the agent mode feature within ChatGPT, designed for completing work on behalf of users in third-party applications and browsers, while Codex is OpenAI’s software coding tool.

One concern with GPT-6.1 Terra is that its more advanced capabilities appear to come at a slight cost in terms of safety. In its blog post, OpenAI said that in nearly 30% of simulated runs, Terra went against restrictions to complete tasks using methods it had no authorization to use.

In addition, OpenAI revealed that GPT-6.1 Terra took unauthorized actions in 13.75% of use cases after coming across messages that came from other AI agents. The company’s system card also shows that researchers found evidence that the model understood it was being tested.

Nonetheless, OpenAI said GPT-6.1 Terra did better in some metrics. For instance, on an internal test built using prompts designed to trick models into making mistakes, its rate of factual errors at low reasoning effort fell to just 16.7%, down from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra. When making maximum effort, its rate of factual errors dropped to just 4.3%.

On the Terminal-Bench 4.0 test, which measures coding agents on tasks done through a computer’s command-line terminal, it solved 50.3% of all tasks when using maximum reasoning effort, up from 21.5% with GPT-5.6 Terra. OpenAI said the model completed these tasks around three-times faster on average than more powerful variants such as GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra.

The release of Terra follows the debut of GPT-6.1 Sol last month. The lineup also includes a lightweight model variant called GPT-6.1 Luna.

# ChatGPT (OpenAI account)

Table of contents

Use your ChatGPT subscription with Docker Agent by signing in with your OpenAI account. No API key needed.

## Overview

Thechatgpt provider authenticates with a ChatGPT account (the same
"Sign in with ChatGPT" flow used by OpenAI's Codex CLI) instead of an
OPENAI_API_KEY. Usage is billed against your ChatGPT Plus, Pro, or
Business plan rather than pay-per-token API credits.

Under the hood, Docker Agent talks to the ChatGPT Codex backend (https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex), which serves the gpt-5 model
family over the OpenAI Responses API. GPT-5.6 (Sol/Terra/Luna) is served
there too; GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.3-Codex are deprecated for ChatGPT sign-in.

## Prerequisites

- A paid ChatGPT subscription (Plus, Pro, or Business).
- A browser on the machine running the sign-in (the OAuth flow uses a fixedlocalhost:1455 callback).

## Sign In
docker agent setup
Pick chatgpt in the provider list: instead of asking for an API key, the wizard opens your browser on the ChatGPT sign-in page and stores the resulting OAuth credential in the Docker Agent config directory (~/.config/cagent/chatgpt-auth.json, owner-only permissions). The access
token is refreshed automatically; you only need to sign in again if the
refresh token is revoked.

Related commands:
docker agent doctor                        # the chatgpt row shows the credential state
rm ~/.config/cagent/chatgpt-auth.json      # sign out (remove the stored sign-in)

## Configuration

### Inline
agents:
  root:
    model: chatgpt/gpt-5.6
    instruction: You are a helpful assistant.

### Named model
models:
  gpt:
    provider: chatgpt
    model: gpt-5.6
    thinking_budget: medium

agents:
  root:
    model: gpt

## Available Models

The Codex backend serves the models available to your ChatGPT plan, typically:

Model | Best For 
---|---
gpt-5.6 | Alias for gpt-5.6-sol; general purpose, strong reasoning 
gpt-5.6-sol | Frontier model, most capable 
gpt-5.6-terra | Everyday workhorse 
gpt-5.6-luna | High-volume, cost-efficient 
gpt-5.2 | Deprecated for ChatGPT sign-in 
gpt-5.2-codex | Deprecated for ChatGPT sign-in 

The effort picker exposes Low/Medium/High/XHigh/Max on the GPT-5.6 family (no Minimal).

## How It Works

- Auth: thedocker agent setup sign-in runs an OAuth 2.0
authorization-code + PKCE flow against auth.openai.com. The stored login
is exposed to credential checks (doctor, first_available, auto model
selection) as the virtual CHATGPT_OAUTH_TOKEN variable.
- API: requests go to the Responses API only; the backend has no Chat Completions endpoint, soapi_type is pinned automatically.
- Request shape: the backend requires stateless requests (store: false)
and a top-level instructions field, so Docker Agent moves system messages
there. Client-side sampling parameters (temperature, top_p,
max_tokens) are not supported by the backend and are dropped.

## Image Input

For image-capable models such asgpt-6.1-sol, you can attach an image:
docker agent run examples/chatgpt-images.yaml --exec \
  --attach examples/chatgpt-images.png "Describe the shapes and colors."
The sample includes a red square centered on a blue background. Running it requires ChatGPT sign-in and access to the selected model. Image input forgpt-6.1-sol is inferred from the matching OpenAI catalogue entry; no
capabilities override is needed.

When models.dev has no directchatgpt/<model> entry, Docker Agent uses the
matching openai/<model> entry for image input only. This applies both to
--attach images and image content returned by MCP tools (for example,
screenshots). Tool images are sent in a follow-up user message alongside the
text function-call output. PDF, audio, and video support, prices, context limits,
tool support, output capabilities, and max_tokens are not inherited.
A direct ChatGPT catalogue entry takes precedence; unknown models remain
text-only.

To intentionally override catalogue capabilities or declare support for an unknown model, see Attachment Capability Overrides. Image input support does not enable image generation or editing.

## Setting the Token Explicitly

CHATGPT_OAUTH_TOKEN can also be set like any other credential (shell
environment, --env-from-file, ...). An explicitly set value takes
precedence over the stored sign-in. This is useful for short-lived CI runs
with a pre-minted access token, but note that such a token expires and is not
refreshed.

## ChatGPT Subscription vs. OpenAI API Key

chatgpt | openai 
---|---
Credential | ChatGPT account sign-in | OPENAI_API_KEY 
Billing | Included in the ChatGPT plan (rate-limited) | Pay per token 
Models | gpt-5 family served by the Codex backend | Full OpenAI API catalog 
Sampling controls (temperature, ...) | Not supported | Supported 
Embeddings / reranking | Not supported | Supported 

When both credentials are configured, automatic model selection prefersopenai; pin --model chatgpt/gpt-5.6 (or use a named model) to use the
subscription.

Note
Use of the Codex backend is governed by OpenAI's terms for ChatGPT and
Codex. Sign-in is per user; do not share the stored credential.

Google.content:
# Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon with cybersecurity focus

Google DeepMind has officially released Gemini 4 Carbon, positioning it as the company's most advanced AI model to date with specialized capabilities in cybersecurity defense and long-horizon coding tasks. Officially launched on October 29, 2026, just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon demonstrates Google's accelerated pace in pushing frontier AI capabilities forward while maintaining deliberate safety controls.

The new model ranks #1 on the recently updated Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 with a score of 59, showing significant improvements across coding, agentic tasks, and cybersecurity benchmarks. Google is initially making Carbon available exclusively to cyber defenders through its Fairwind Program before expanding access to broader developer, business, and consumer audiences.

## Benchmark Performance and Cybersecurity Leadership

Gemini 4 Carbon establishes state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. The model achieves 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for vulnerability detection, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation testing, and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching capabilities. These scores represent substantial gains over existing frontier models in security-critical tasks.

On internal benchmarks, Carbon delivers more than 2x uplift in generating secure code compared to Argon, its predecessor released in early October 2026. The Chrome team at Google reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another major lab's frontier model when generating high-quality security patches. Wiz, a leading cloud security platform, observed Carbon leading benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for the company's Scan for Good initiative.

## Long-Horizon Agentic Workflows

Carbon is engineered for sustained agentic workflows that tackle complex, multi-step engineering problems over extended periods. According to Google, internal teams have observed the model running for days to persist through dead ends and solve intricate tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

The model also demonstrates strong improvements in full-stack web development. Carbon jumped +89 elo points to rank #4 at 1768 on WebDev Arena, reflecting enhanced quality of output and artifacts in web development tasks. These gains extend to multimodal understanding and scientific reasoning tasks, making Carbon a versatile tool for technical teams.

## Pricing and Availability Timeline

Gemini 4 Carbon launches at the same introductory pricing as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input tokens are priced at 95% off the standard input token rate, making extended context operations more economical for developers working on large-scale projects.

Google is taking a phased rollout approach, beginning with a subset of cyber defenders this week. The company is actively participating in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing and gathering feedback to iterate on guardrails. Broader availability to developers, businesses, and consumers through Google's product surfaces is planned for as soon as possible following the initial testing phase.

## Safety Architecture and Alignment Improvements

Carbon builds on the multi-layered safety and security stack introduced with Argon, combining model training techniques, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. Google reports making significant strides in model alignment, training Carbon to respond appropriately to complex or high-pressure tasks.

The company documented Argon's alignment propensities in its Safety and Security report released earlier in October 2026. With Carbon, Google challenged itself to achieve further improvements in alignment behavior. Internal evaluations show reduced misalignment and fabrication rates in live coding environments compared to earlier models.

## What This Means

Gemini 4 Carbon represents a significant step forward in AI-powered cybersecurity defense and software engineering capabilities. The model's state-of-the-art performance on security benchmarks, combined with its ability to sustain complex workflows over days, positions it as a powerful tool for technical teams facing increasingly sophisticated security challenges. Google's deliberate rollout strategy, prioritizing cyber defenders before general availability, reflects a measured approach to deploying advanced AI capabilities while maintaining safety standards. As organizations continue to grapple with growing cybersecurity threats, Carbon's specialized capabilities could reshape how security teams detect, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities at scale.

Google.content:
# Google DeepMind’s Genie 4 builds AI worlds that talk and change on command

Gemini models plan and check each step as a Genie 4 world runs. Trusted testers get it first, then Google AI Ultra subscribers and developers.

Google DeepMind has released Genie 4, a world model that builds photorealistic worlds in real time. They come with sound, and with characters that speak. It opened to trusted testers as a research preview on 27 October, the lab said in a blog post.

Users steer a simulation with text prompts as it runs, changing the weather, moving the camera or adding a person or object. DeepMind says it is its first real-time world model to generate audio natively. That includes music, ambient noise and dialogue that reacts to the user.

“Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI,” the DeepMind team wrote.

## Gemini in the loop

Genie 4 builds on Google’s Gemini models. Gemini Omni anchors how the worlds look and behave. Gemini 3.8 Flash works as an agent in the loop. It watches the scene, breaks a goal into steps and checks each new frame to confirm that a step worked.

In one experiment, Gemini 4 Argon, the model Google released publicly this month, planned a task for Genie 4 to simulate: Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid playing checkers. DeepMind says this opens up endless training scenarios for robots.

Scenes now stay consistent for up to two minutes, double Genie 3’s limit, Rebecca Bellan reported for TechCrunch. The lab says physics such as aerodynamics and collisions are more realistic, and that people move more naturally.

“What we’ll increasingly see in the future are these hybrid world models, where you have a combination of Gemini writing code and text, and Genie ingesting that in real time and simulating reality at different levels of abstraction,” Tejas Kulkarni, a research director at Google, said in a briefing, according to TechCrunch.

## Who gets it, and when

Testers in film, journalism, education, gaming and engineering have used the model for previsualisation and game prototypes, according to DeepMind. Photojournalists have tried turning archival photos into simulations. Next, it comes to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie. Early partners will get it in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. DeepMind has opened a waitlist but gave no date.

Ultra plans start at $100 a month, Ryan Whitwam wrote for Ars Technica. Ars also noted that the reveal of Genie 3 last year sent gaming stocks tumbling.

DeepMind lists limits. Details and object permanence can drift as a simulation runs longer or after several prompt edits. Legible text and audio accuracy are still in development. All video and audio from Genie 4 carries SynthID, Google’s invisible watermark.

The release comes as the world model field consolidates. AMD agreed to buy World Labs. Amazon has been in talks to buy Decart, and Rivian bought Third Dimension for driving simulation.

## Gemini 4 Carbon can autonomously detect and fix security vulnerabilities

Unlike general-purpose conversational models, Carbon is optimised to run multi-day reasoning loops focused on identifying code vulnerabilities, validating their exploitability and drafting remediations.
While Gemini 4 Argon targeted general reasoning and developer workflows, Carbon is tailored to defensive security and autonomous software remediation.

Google confirmed Carbon will launch on its Gemini API at an introductory rate of USD2.00 (~RM8.13) per million input tokens and USD10.00 (~RM40.64) per million output tokens, before shifting to standard rates of USD4.00 (~RM16.26) and USD20.00 (~RM81.28).

Cached input tokens carry a 95 percent discount, reducing the introductory caching cost to USD 0.10 (~RM 0.41) per million tokens, and USD 0.20 (~RM 0.81) once standard pricing takes effect. The discount targets enterprise developers running repetitive, multi-repository codebases through automated security sweeps.

The introductory pricing structure matches Argon, positioning Carbon to compete directly on operational costs against frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

## How Gemini 4 Carbon compares with other AI models

On third-party evaluations, Carbon is ranked first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 with an aggregate score of 59, narrowly passing Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra.

Google reported the model led 15 of 17 standard benchmark evaluations, trailing competitors only in software engineering on FrontierSWE 2 and computer use on OSWorld-2.1.

The architecture focuses heavily on the vulnerability remediation lifecycle across three distinct stages: discovery, validation and remediation. Carbon recorded an 88.2% score on SEC-bench Pro for detecting security flaws across codebases, followed by 54.8% on ExploitGym for evaluating exploitability and 71.0% on CWE-bench for automated patch generation.

Google DeepMind claimed Carbon produced viable security fixes at more than twice the rate of Argon. Google also claimed that Carbon achieved more than twice the success rate of Argon in generating secure code. Meanwhile, its Chrome team reported that Carbon performed over 10 times better than a competing frontier model at generating high-quality software patches.

## How reliable is Gemini 4 Carbon against cyber attacks?

Google DeepMind reported zero successful attacks against Carbon on Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, down from a 0.7 percent breach rate recorded by Argon.

The company also measured a 26 percent reduction in operational overreach actions taken outside user-defined parameters and a 29 percent decline in under-service, where agents abandon multi-step tasks before completion.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Carbon reduced successful environment exploits and rule-breaking shortcuts to 0.0 percent, with total attempts dropping to 0.4 percent. In internal testing, DeepMind stated the model halved unsupported claims relative to Argon.

Third-party testing by Artificial Analysis placed Carbon first on its AA-Omniscience evaluation with a score of 54. The firm recorded an 11 percent hallucination rate for Carbon, rising from Argon’s 4 percent but well below the 50 percent rates registered by both Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra.

## No specified timeline or launch date for the public

Google is restricting initial access to Carbon to a subset of cybersecurity defenders beginning this week. The company will gradually expand access to additional trusted partners through its Fairwind Program, an initiative that provides early model access to select government bodies, critical infrastructure operators and enterprise defense teams.

Google also confirmed it is participating in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. The company plans to gather defender feedback and refine safety controls before rolling out Carbon to developers, enterprise clients and consumers across Vertex AI, the Gemini API and the Gemini consumer application. A general availability date has not been announced.

### Google debuts flagship Gemini 4 Carbon model with cybersecurity upgrades

Google LLC today debuted Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier large language model adept at complex programming tasks.

The LLM is rolling out just two weeks after the search introduced its previous flagship LLM, Gemini 4 Argon. According to Google, internal tests have shown Carbon to be more than twice as good at generating secure code. Additionally, the model outperforms GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Carbon’s most notable benchmark result is its record score on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It’s a test that combines more than a half-dozen popular LLM evaluations. Google tested Carbon on a new version of the index that was publicly released today. It includes two additional benchmarks and removes a number of saturated questions, questions deemed too easy for frontier models.

Carbon is particularly adept at cybersecurity tasks. It handily beat the previous record on SEC-bench Pro, which evaluates LLMs’ ability to find weak points in complex software systems. The model is also better than its predecessor at patching the vulnerabilities it finds.

“The Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab’s large frontier model when generating high-quality patches,” Koray Kavukcuoglu, the senior vice president of Google DeepMind and Google’s chief artificial intelligence architect, wrote in a blog post.

Argon, the company’s previous flagship LLM, includes guardrails designed to mitigate hallucinations and cyberattacks. Google implemented an improved version of that feature set in Carbon. According to the company, a number of internal teams that use Carbon in “live coding environments” reported a nearly 80% drop in misalignment alerts.

When LLMs struggle to answer a user question, they sometimes fill their knowledge gaps by hallucinating inaccurate information. Google configured Carbon to avoid such behavior.

“In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon,” Kavukcuoglu wrote. “It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.”

Alignment issues can also crop up while a model is being trained. Developers train frontier LLMs by giving them a large number of tasks similar to the ones they’ll be expected to perform in production. LLMs sometimes cheat on those tasks, which is not conducive to the learning process.

Google tested whether Carbon would use shortcuts to solve the coding challenges in the Terminal-Bench 4.0 benchmark. The model attempted to cheat across only 0.4% of the questions and none of the attempts were successful. Carbon performed even better on the Gray Swan IPI Benchmark, which tests LLMs’ susceptibility to indirect prompt injections. The model blocked all of the simulated prompt injections.

The company will make Carbon available later this week through its Fairwind Program, which gives organizations such as internet providers early access to its LLMs. Participants use the models to fix cybersecurity flaws in their systems. Google plans to refine Carbon’s guardrails based on feedback from early adopters before making it broadly available.
